title: Quantifying the Accuracy and Precision of the Transition Dipole Moment Alignment from Realistic Angular Emission Data.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Introduction From solar cells to light emitting diodes
to sensors, the efficiency
of every optoelectronic device is inherently influenced by the angular
emission pattern of light. In photovoltaics, the maximum voltage and
efficiency of a solar cell is dictated by the etendue, or angular
spread of light emission from radiative recombination of the semiconductor.
Up to 10% in efficiency can be gained when the angular spread of light
from the sun is matched by the angular spread of light emitted by
the radiative recombination of the solar cell. 
 , 
  In
lighting and displays, the angular light emission determines how much
light is emitted from the device and defines the external quantum
efficiency (EQE). For example, organic light emitting diodes (OLEDs)
lose up to 80% of generated photons when light is emitted isotropically
as some light is emitted into angles that are trapped within the device
layers instead of emitted outward for viewing. 
 − 
 
 
  Thus, to maximize the efficiency
of these devices, we must maximize light emission into desired angles
and modes. Light emission is an inherently directional process.  Photons are generated during radiative recombination,
where electrons relax from higher energy to lower energy states. The
electron’s cycling between different energy levels generates
an inherent dipole moment (the transition dipole moment, or TDM) and
an anisotropic electric field, resulting in anisotropic light emission.
This directionality is not observed in many bulk materials: most bulk
materials have many energetic states with equal strengths in all directions,
thus resulting in a completely isotropic emission pattern. However,
this directionality can be observed in materials that only support
individual states, such as dye molecules,  in materials with confined, quantized states, such as quantum dots 
 , 
  and 2D films,  and in nanomaterials
that are highly responsive to their environment. 
 − 
 
 
  Using these directionally emitting
materials in optoelectronic devices can overcome the entropic losses
discussed earlier and yield significant device efficiency gains. 
 , − 
 
 
 The angular light emission pattern, 
 , , − 
 , − 
 
 
  light absorption or emission polarization, 
 , 
  and photoluminescence lifetime 
 − 
 
 
  all provide insight into the
alignment and relative strength of the transition dipole moments of
a sample. Resolving the effective dipole alignment through the angular
emission pattern is a popular method for characterizing simple thin
film samples, for example by (1) using a light detector that directly
collects the light emission at different angles;  or (2) inserting a simple lens into the pathway of a microscope
that changes the focal plane to the Fourier plane of the microscope,
providing a 2D projection of the 3D angular emission pattern, known
as back focal plane imaging or momentum-resolved spectroscopy.  The fitted transition dipole moment from this
measurement represents the statistical average of all the transition
dipole moments in the emitting layer. For a simple optical environment,
such as a thin emissive layer
(film thickness ≪ emission wavelength) on a planar substrate,
the angular emission pattern is well-described by a 1D analytical
solution that modifies the dipole emission pattern by interaction
with the two interfaces (film-vacuum, film–substrate) and propagation
through the film. Example projections of angular emission patterns
for various dipole alignments are shown in  Figure  
 C. The dipole alignment is typically determined
by finding the best fit between the experimental angular emission
pattern and the calculated patterns of various dipole alignments.
However, the best fit is not always obvious:  Figure  
 C shows that the angular emission patterns
look very similar when the dipole is aligned more parallel to the
substrate. This can be a significant challenge for predicting the
device performance; even very subtle changes in the anisotropy of
the electric dipoles can have an immense impact on the device efficiency.
For example, the external quantum efficiency of an OLED is 24.7% higher
for an emitter where the effective dipole alignment angle is 8°
closer to the substrate than a purely isotropic emitter (average effective
angle 35.3°).  Despite this range
in performance, the uncertainty of this fitting procedure is typically
not reported. Further, the inherent or expected error of this fitting
procedure has not yet been widely quantified. Therefore, there is
a great need to not only determine the dipole alignments of candidate
materials but also to know the precision of these dipole alignments
to give an accurate prediction and range of device performance. 1 (a) 3-layer
schematic showing air, the emissive film, and substrate.
The effective transition dipole moment (TDM eff ) angle is
the angle between the substrate and the in-plane and out-of-plane
dipole contributions. The thickness of the film (D) is assumed to
be smaller than the emission wavelength of light (λ). The dashed
pink lines represent the in-plane and out-of-plane dipoles that contribute
to the effective transition dipole moment. (b) 3D angular emission
pattern (black wireframe) from a dipole (purple arrow) in free space.
Emission is defined in spherical coordinates (θ. ϕ). (c)
Projected x-polarized angular emission patterns of a dipole from the
3-layer model for different TDM eff  angle orientations with
respect to the normalized momentum vectors  k 
 
 x 
 ,  k 
 
 y 
 . The toroid-shape of the dipole is modified by the air–film
and film–substrate interfaces. The angular emission pattern
appears very similar for low effective transition dipole moment angles
(TDM eff  ≤ 30°). In this work, we apply a statistical method to
evaluate the accuracy
and precision of measuring the dipole alignment from the fitting to
angular emission patterns. First, we quantify the fundamental precision
for this type of measurement using Monte Carlo simulations to add
random noise to theoretical angular emission patterns. We show that
the confidence intervals are not constant across samples, and there
is an increased associated uncertainty for films with most dipoles
aligned close to the substrate and for films with higher refractive
index ( n 
 2  ≥ 3). Next, we explore
the inherent difficulties of finding an accurate fit, or where the
best fit data set matches the correct underlying parameters. We show
that accurately determining the correct transition dipole moment alignment
is possible, albeit challenging, when additional parameters of the
emitting layer are unknown (thickness, refractive index) using rigorous
optimization methods such as simulated annealing. Finally, we show
that pixel bleeding and blurring that typically appear in experimental
angular emission patterns obfuscate the true transition dipole moment
alignment from the experimentally best-fit values, preventing accurate
characterization. We showed that incorporating such nonidealities
in angular emission patterns can lead to enormous differences (>10°)
between the best fit effective TDM angle and the true effective TDM
angle, and this is exacerbated again for thin films with high refractive
indices ( n 
 2  ≥ 2). We offer an improved
and physics-motivated protocol for processing experimental data by
selecting a specific subset of the angular emission data, which allows
us to achieve much more accurate fits than the traditional methods
of fitting just the p-polarized linecuts or the entire angular space.
Thus, this work provides a procedure both for quantifying the precision
of characterizing the transition dipole moment alignment and for ensuring
more accurate alignment measurements when experimental nonidealities
are present.

sections.heading: The Generation of Theoretical Angular Emission Patterns
sections.text:
The Generation of Theoretical Angular Emission Patterns In this work, we used artificially generated data sets of the photoluminescence
intensity as a function of photon momentum and several underlying
parameters. These data sets can then be fed into subsequent statistical
models to quantify accuracy and precision. The angular light emission
pattern from dipoles within a thin film is well described by a simple
three-layer analytical model. 
 , , , , 
 
 Figure  
 A shows the
setup with the three layers: (1) the background media (usually assumed
to be air), (2) the emissive thin film where the thickness of the
film is smaller than the wavelength of emitted light, and (3) the
substrate (usually glass). This analysis is generalized to assume
that horizontal dipole contributions are degenerate, meaning there
are horizontal dipoles along the x- and  y -directions.
Most derivations assume a polarizer is used during the measurement
because this removes one of the horizontal dipole contributions (here
applied in the  x -direction) and allows the average
dipole orientation, or the difference between horizontal and vertical
dipole contributions, be better resolved. Here, we use the following
general equation for the polarized light emission intensity projected
onto a 2-D collection plane ( N

by TDM eff  =

 . In this scheme, TDM eff  = 0°
corresponds to completely in-plane dipole contributions, TDM eff  = 35.3° corresponds to isotropic dipole contributions, and
TDM eff  = 90° corresponds to completely out-of-plane
dipole contributions. Importantly, TDM eff  here does not

for thin films of many emitters with the transition dipole moment

 B). This uniform emission pattern is then
modified by the reflection and transmission through the surrounding
interfaces. Example x-polarized angular emission patterns for different
TDM eff  angles are provided in  Figure  
 C. We include the x-polarizer to better resolve

horizontal dipoles. Lower TDM eff  angles (aligned parallel
to substrate) have strong minima along the  k

in the center ( k

generated data sets were then compared against the basic theory to
quantify the inherent accuracy and precision of this technique.

an anisotropic electric field, resulting in anisotropic light emission.
This directionality is not observed in many bulk materials: most bulk
materials have many energetic states with equal strengths in all directions,
thus resulting in a completely isotropic emission pattern. However,
this directionality can be observed in materials that only support
individual states, such as dye molecules,  in materials with confined, quantized states, such as quantum dots 
 , 
  and 2D films,  and in nanomaterials
that are highly responsive to their environment.

intervals changing as a
function of transition dipole moment angle, we also observed that
the inherent confidence intervals are not constant across different

This increasing error with increasing refractive index and decreasing
thickness can be explained by the photonic density of states. The
photonic density of states of a medium is tied to its refractive index:
the higher the refractive index, the more light modes the medium can
support. Therefore, as the refractive index of the emissive film (n 2 ) increases beyond the refractive index of the substrate (n 3 ), more light is coupled into parallel propagating modes instead
of forward modes toward collection, reducing the amount of photoluminescence
collected and making it more difficult to distinguish between angular
emission patterns. We attribute the more robust fitting behavior for
thicker films to the scaling of the ρ

contribution, which scales approximately as  D 
 2 . This increases the change in the angular emission pattern
as the angle increases, giving more consistent fits and smaller confidence
intervals. The conclusion that there is a higher inherent uncertainty
for lower transition dipole moment angles and higher refractive indices
poses a significant challenge for both fundamental and applied research
for semiconductors, whose refractive indices often ranges between
2.0 – 3.0 or even higher. For example, light emitting diodes
and displays need a lower transition dipole moment angle to increase
the amount of light emitted out of the film. However, quantifying
the angle of semiconductors with a low transition dipole moment angle,
especially thinner, quantum materials, will always be more difficult,
leading to more variation and uncertainty in predicting full device
efficiencies. Finally, we investigated the impact of the number
of fitting parameters.
While thickness and refractive index can be a straightforward characterization
for highly uniform vacuum deposition techniques, other materials,
such as colloidally grown semiconductor nanostructures, may have variation
in refractive index (e.g., nanoparticle packing) or thickness  that make it harder to quantify. Fitting all
three parameters from the angle-resolve photoluminescence data alone
is not recommended, and many other methods exist to characterize the
film thickness and refractive index independently (ellipsometry, atomic
force microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, etc.). However, this
analysis may be useful when comparing many similar films of nanoparticles,
where the refractive index across the sample varies dramatically due
to effects like particle aggregation.  Figure

effective transition dipole moment angle and film thickness are unknown,
and all three are unknown. Intuitively, fitting more parameters widens
the confidence interval, as the best fit parameters are allowed to
stray further in the parameter space from the underlying theory. Interestingly,
both two-parameter cases do not share the same confidence intervals,
with unknown film thickness appearing to play a larger role in widening
the confidence interval than the refractive index. This is especially
notable in  Figure

nearly double in width at effective transition dipole moment angles

Supporting  Figures S1, S7–S9  show
these results for different combinations of refractive index (n 2  = 1, 1.5, 2, 3) and thickness (D = 10 nm, 20 nm, 50 nm, 100
nm) for different fit parameters. The same trends mostly hold, but
there are some cases where the confidence intervals do not increase
monotonically with decreasing transition dipole moment angle, (for
example, n2 = 1.5, D = 10 nm). We attribute this to the nonlinear
nature of the underlying theory, causing certain angular emission
patterns to change less as a function of the transition dipole moment
angle at different angles. We conclude that fitting to multiple parameters
will yield very high uncertainties, especially in the cases of thin,
high refractive index films which already have high inherent errors
from fitting the transition dipole moment angle. It is therefore vitally
important to verify the emitting layer thickness and refractive index
independently to avoid extremely imprecise results.

Accurately Characterizing the Transition Dipole Moment Alignment
Depends on Precise Knowledge of the Emissive Film Parameters With the inherent error of this process quantified, we next investigated
the accuracy limitations of determining the effective transition dipole
moment angle from an angular emission pattern. In the previous section,
calculation of the confidence intervals always started from the true
transition dipole moment angle. However, finding the true transition
dipole moment angle from a data set is not always straightforward.
Typically, this process is done via χ 2  minimization
( 
 χ 2 = ∑ ( experimental − theory ) 2 variance 
 ). The χ 2  is calculated
by comparing the experimental angular emission pattern to the theoretically
generated angular emission patterns for all possible fitting parameters.
The assigned transition dipole moment angle occurs for the smallest
χ 2  value. Here, we used a theoretically generated
angular emission pattern as our experimental data set. This allowed
us to evaluate the inherent accuracy of finding the transition dipole
moment angle from the angular emission pattern while knowing the true
value of this angle. So far, finding the true transition dipole
moment angle from the
χ 2  minimization of the angular emission pattern is
trivial when it is the only unknown parameter: the minimum χ 2  always occurs at the true angle (i.e., the transition dipole
moment angle that was used to generate the data). However, analysis
of the χ 2  value for multiple fitting parameters (e.g.,
angle and thickness, angle and refractive index) shows there can be
numerous local minima for a realistic domain. This results in conventional
minimization methods frequently finding a local minimum that does
not correspond to the true underlying parameters the theory was generated
from.  Figure

random noise. These nonidealities can lead to angular emission patterns
looking slightly blurred, especially at the maxima and minima of the
sample.

Conclusion and Outlook In this work, we provided a
methodology ( Figure  
 A and  Supporting Methods ) to quantify
the precision of determining the transition dipole
moment alignment from an angular emission pattern by studying artificially
generated data sets. Additionally, we explored methods to ensure the
minimum of the χ 2  function was accurately found even
when there are uncertainties or unknowns in the emissive film properties
of thickness and refractive index. For the case where statistical
noise is the only nonideality, we showed that an accurate fit can
theoretically be determined without prior knowledge of the emissive
layer’s thickness or refractive index. However, in practice,
it is likely much easier to independently measure the emissive layer’s
properties to eliminate local minima that can lead to highly incorrect
transition dipole moment alignment fits. Further, we showed that the
inherent error of this measurement is not equal across all samples.
The uncertainty of determining the transition dipole moment angle
generally increases for more horizontally aligned samples and this
is exacerbated for thin samples with high refractive indices. This
effect was magnified as realistic nonidealities were applied to the
generated angular emission patterns. Blurring of the extrema, which
is typically seen in experimental samples, showed that fitting low
effective transition dipole moment angles could become highly inaccurate.
Some best fit angles deviated from their true values by as much as
10°-30° for higher refractive indices (n 2  = 2.0
– 3.0) when fitting either to a single cross-section, as is
typical in prior works, or over the entire angular emission pattern.
However, we were able to show much more accurate fits when selectively
fitting to a subset of the angular emission data. When focusing on
photon emission angles that are more susceptible to changes in the
transition dipole moment alignment, we showed that best fit typically
occurred within 5° of the true angle, a huge improvement over
the previous fitting methods. Thus, our work highlighted a previously
undiscussed challenge: it is more difficult to accurately quantify
the transition dipole moment angle for thin film semiconductor samples
(nanocrystals, 2D semiconductors, thin films, etc.) with mostly horizontal
dipole contributions (low transition dipole moment angles). Further,
we developed a new protocol to ensure a more accurate fit, which is
especially important to new materials where the transition dipole
moment alignment is not well-known. The importance of this work
spans across both fundamental and applied
research. The statistical methods described here can finally enable
the reporting of the  range  of the extracted transition
dipole moment angle. Not only can this provide better quantification
between experiment and theory for the development of new materials,
but this can also provide a more realistic range of device efficiency.
However, this work also showed the limitations of using the angular
emission pattern, regardless of the measurement type, to determine
the transition dipole moment angle. Not only is it harder to fit lower
transition dipole moment angles, but also the fundamental uncertainty
increases and the fit becomes more inaccurate for realistic data for
thin film, semiconductor samples (n 2  ≥ 2.0). This
will be a significant challenge for understanding the electronic properties
of new quantum confined materials, such as nanocrystals and 2D semiconductors.
Additionally, any device that relies on maximizing light emission
into forward propagating modes will have a much more difficult time
predicting performance when semiconductor samples are used as the
emissive layer. Our new protocol of fitting over a selected range
of data (“bowtie” pattern) alleviates this for most
orientations and materials, but there are still a few cases where
the inaccuracy is high. More research is needed to develop methods
to improve the accuracy or corroborate the value of the apparent transition
dipole moment angle, as this parameter will be necessary for the future
optoelectronic device design and fundamental materials characterization.
